The two foreign ministers also discussed new EU sanctions, Ukraine’s membership bid and the need for greater pressure on Moscow. by Kyiv Post | July 24, 2026, 3:59 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied A man passes in front of the entrance on the second day of the Ukraine Recovery Conference (URC 2026) hosted by the Poland’s Prime Minister in Gdansk, Poland, on June 26, 2026. (Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and his Polish counterpart Radosław Sikorski discussed Russia’s escalating attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea on Thursday, warning that the strikes threaten not only Ukraine but global food supplies. Sybiha described the conversation with Poland’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister as productive, with the two officials focusing on Russia’s intensifying campaign against civilian vessels and Ukrainian port infrastructure. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “We discussed Russia’s intensified attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea and the implications of this terror for global food security,” Sybiha wrote on X . The conversation comes as Russian attacks increasingly threaten Ukraine’s main maritime export route. Advertisement Between June 20 and July 20, Russian forces attacked 28 civilian vessels in the Black Sea, killing 21 people, according to regional prosecutors. Some shipowners have since halted calls at Ukrainian ports amid mounting security concerns, disrupting agricultural exports. On July 20, a Russian missile strike hit the Guinea-Bissau-flagged Golden Leo, which was carrying corn near Odesa, killing 10 people. A day later, a Liberian-flagged vessel sailing toward Ukraine was struck off the Romanian coast, further highlighting the growing risks to international commercial shipping in the region. Russia acknowledged on Wednesday that its forces had struck ports and vessels in Odesa and Chornomorsk, claiming the targets were supporting Ukraine’s military. Other Topics of Interest Russian FIDE Chief Steps Aside After EU Sanctions Over Ukraine Brussels linked Arkady Dvorkovich to support for Russia’s occupation policies and undertaking chess activities in seized Ukrainian territories. EU sanctions and Ukraine’s membership bid Sybiha and Sikorski also welcomed the European Union’s adoption of its long-awaited 21st sanctions package against Russia. The measures, formally approved Thursday, target Russia’s energy, financial and cryptocurrency sectors and add 218 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions list – the bloc’s largest batch of individual listings in four years. Sybiha described the package as a decision Ukraine had been waiting for and stressed the need to continue increasing economic pressure on Moscow. Advertisement The two foreign ministers also discussed Ukraine’s progress toward EU membership. Sybiha thanked Poland for supporting the opening of negotiating Clusters 1 and 6. Cluster 1, covering the fundamental reforms required for EU membership, was opened in June. Cluster 6, covering external relations as well as aspects of foreign, security and defense policy, followed on July 14. More pressure on Moscow Sybiha also briefed Sikorski on Russia’s latest large-scale strikes against Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, with the two ministers discussing the need for additional pressure on Moscow. The Ukrainian foreign minister thanked Poland for its support since the first days of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The call brought together several issues Kyiv has increasingly sought to link diplomatically – protecting Black Sea trade, tightening economic sanctions on Moscow, advancing Ukraine’s EU integration and maintaining Western pressure as Russia continues its attacks. Afghanistan Taliban threaten former Afghan police worker after MoD leak reveals identity UK has refused resettlement application despite ‘years of loyal service’ that have resulted in ‘constant fear’ of reprisals Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent Sun 16 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man has received threats from the Taliban after his work for the Afghan police was revealed by a Ministry of Defence leak and the UK refused his application for resettlement. Hamid* worked for the Afghan national police special unit and received certificates for his work signed by senior British figures praising his “dedication, unparalleled service and leadership”. His details were also included in an accidental 2022 leak by an MoD official that identified 18,700 Afghans who had worked with or for the British government. Hamid said he had received a number of threats from the Taliban , including a video he shared with the Guardian in which a man cradling a rifle and sitting below a Taliban flag threatens to pursue him and cites knowledge of his previous movements. View image in fullscreen Taliban security personnel in Kandahar. It is nearly five years since the group retook political power in Afghanistan. Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/Getty Images The MoD, however, has rejected his application for resettlement under the Afghan relocations and assistance policy (Arap) scheme. His most recent rejection, received on 31 July, stated that Hamid had not provided evidence of “working alongside, in partnership with or closely supporting a UK government department”. It gave him 28 days to appeal. Hamid said: “This is extremely painful because I have already submitted every document available to me proving my service. Furthermore, many of my former colleagues who served in exactly the same department and performed the same duties have already been relocated to the UK through the Arap scheme. “Despite this evidence, my case continues to be refused. I believe my case raises serious questions about how some former Afghan partners of the UK continue to be treated despite years of loyal service.” Hamid’s plea for help comes five years after the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on 15 August 2021 after the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. The UK government launched the Arap scheme on 1 April 2021 and closed it to new applications on 1 July last year. Pre-existing applications continue to be processed. View image in fullscreen Hamid lives in hiding and says the emotional impact has been ‘devastating’. Under Arap, high risk of death or serious injury are only taken into account if the rest of the criteria are deemed to have been met, which they have not in Hamid’s case. “Must I wait until I am captured, tortured or killed by the Taliban before my service and the danger I face are finally recognised?” he said. Abbas fought the Taliban alongside US and Australian troops. Now exiled in Iran, he feels abandoned Read more “Following the Ministry of Defence data breach, my personal information was exposed, placing me at even greater risk. Since then, my life has changed completely. I cannot safely leave my home to work. I live in constant fear of being recognised or targeted.” After the leak, the then defence secretary, John Healey, said the dataset included people who had made speculative applications under Arap and had not worked with British forces. He said being included in the leak “ doesn’t give them a right to claim access to Britain ”. “It doesn’t give them a right to claim asylum. It doesn’t make them eligible for the special [Arap] scheme that Britain put in place for those who’d worked alongside or served with our forces,” he said. Hamid said that because he was in hiding he had no reliable income and relied on his wife, who supports the family by doing small jobs from home. “This is our family’s only source of income, and even then we struggle simply to survive,” he said. “The emotional impact has been devastating. My wife and I have become deeply exhausted, depressed and hopeless after years of fear, uncertainty, repeated refusals and financial hardship. “I am not asking for special treatment. I am only asking for a fair review based on the evidence I have already provided.” An MoD spokesperson said: “Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis, assessed against the evidence provided, such as how they supported the UK mission in Afghanistan , and in line with the publicly available eligibility criteria. “Since the Taliban takeover, the UK has resettled almost 39,000 Afghan men, women and children through Afghan resettlement schemes.” Name has been changed Explore more on these topics Afghanistan Taliban Ministry of Defence South and central Asia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Seaman Apprentice Andrew Novak/US Navy US military US Navy destroyer adrift in South China Sea for four days after losing power USS Benfold lost power after ‘engineering casualty’ leaving sailors without galley services, toilets and air conditioning Edward Helmore Mon 17 Aug 2026 14.09 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 14.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A US guided-missile destroyer reportedly spent four days adrift and without power in the South China Sea in July, furthering concerns about strain being placed on deployed military members. The USS Benfold, an Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer which had been sailing with the George Washington Carrier Strike Group, was reported to have been towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines, according to the US Naval Institute News, an independent military publication. The 10,000-ton destroyer lost power after what a spokesperson with the US seventh fleet called “an engineering casualty involving its generators”, resulting in a loss of power. That loss of power meant sailors were without galley services, toilets and air conditioning, Commander Matthew Comer told USNI News in a statement. Another vessel, USS Robert Smalls, the cruiser attached to the strike group, had to help provide meals for the crew. Comer said that the Benfield lost power on 24 July and was towed on 28 July. Power was restored two days later. Families of US sailors denounce Trump and Hegseth for ‘dismissing their experiences and calling them liars’ Read more “There were no injuries to the crew, who demonstrated resilience, grit, professionalism and unwavering steadiness in their response,” Comer’s statement to USNI News said. The Guardian has reached out to theseventh fleet for comment. The USS George Washington strike group on Monday was headed to the Middle East to relive the USS Abraham Lincoln, a carrier that in recent days was subject to reports by the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes of multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard after more than 200 days without a port call. That has prompted Democratic lawmakers and military families to demand that the Trump administration answer questions about low morale, mental health challenges and living conditions for crew members. US senator Ruben Gallego, an Arizona Democrat and retired marine, said on ABC News on Sunday that the problems arose from the Iran war that the Trump administration started in February but has not been able to resolve. The Lincoln originally deployed to the Indo-Pacific before being ordered to sail to the Middle East in January. “The deep, deep, deep problem here is that this administration did not plan for this war, did not plan how to get out of this war, and did not really understand how this war was going to escalate,” he said. The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has rejected the accounts, calling them “completely misrepresented”. “We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” he told Newsmax, adding that sailors in “austere conditions with less port calls” were doing “incredible” work. The Navy, meanwhile, has said: “Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship. “We know that extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make in support of our nation’s security,” Navy officials said in a statement obtained by Task & Purpose. In an opinion piece published by the Wall Street Journal on Sunday, Adm Brad Cooper, commander of US Central Command, said he had been onboard the Lincoln in the Arabian Gulf a day earlier and addressed the sailors. Cooper said he had made the trip to “see how its 4,000-plus service members are doing and thank them for their extraordinary resilience in the face of constant pressure” and called it “an amazing visit”. He acknowledged the media reports on the ships “operational tempo, crew morale and the realities facing our deployed forces” and said what he found “is that many elements of those stories are old news”. The crew is tired, but they continue to fire on all cylinders,” he wrote. “History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era.” In a post on X Monday, Cooper said that of the Navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health. “This doesn’t mean all is perfect,” he wrote. “Find any of the nearly 4 million Navy veterans today and they will likely tell you that service at sea for long periods isn’t for everyone. It’s uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways.” The Guardian on Sunday reported on families who have had loved ones deployed for months on US warships amid the Iran war and were furious with the Trump administration’s dismissal of their concerns about the pressures and conditions at issue. “It’s a feeling of betrayal,” the sister of a Lincoln crew member said in that report. “These are frustrating, false and careless comments, and they are going to have a lot of consequences for my brother.” Explore more on these topics US military Trump administration US-Israel war on Iran US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty Images Australian immigration and asylum Albanese vows refugee intake won’t be slashed after earlier reports of Coalition-level cut Prime minister intervenes amid anger at news Tony Burke was planning to cut intake of 20,000 arrivals by a third Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Thu 27 Aug 2026 04.06 EDT First published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Anthony Albanese has guaranteed Australia’s annual refugee intake will not be cut next financial year, shutting down plans for the arrivals quota to drop by one-third to Coalition-era levels. Labor MPs and refugee advocates reacted angrily to news on Thursday morning that the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, was planning to cut intake of 20,000 arrivals to 13,750 in 2027-28. By late afternoon, the prime minister confirmed the change would not proceed. News of the plan coincided with efforts by Labor to drive down migration levels amid increasing political pressure from One Nation . “The refugee intake needs to be renewed in the coming budget as the 20,000 places was available for 4 years,” Albanese said in a statement. “This intake number remains government policy and will be continued in future years, consistent with Australia’s humanitarian commitments and sits beside our strong border security measures.” One Nation’s immigration policy is hard to define – even by its own MPs Read more Migration settings are the subject of an internal fight within Labor, as the government seeks to bring net overseas migration down to 225,000 next financial year. Burke had delayed announcing the broader policy earlier this month. Rules for backpackers will be tightened, including working holidaymaker settings for Britons coming to Australia. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Earlier, when asked about the refugee intake changes on Thursday, Albanese hinted some of the reporting was incorrect and said Labor was responding to post-pandemic fluctuations. “We’re worried about trying to get numbers right,” the prime minister said at a regional summit in Dubbo. “We’re responding to national needs,” he said. “There is a current spike in the support for One Nation, quite clearly, but we’ve responded. We started lowering the numbers well before that occurred because we recognise that we want to get that right to assist the Australian economy.” In 2015, Labor’s national conference committed the party to accepting 27,000 refugees a year by 2025, part of a heated debate over asylum seeker policy and boat turnbacks. At the party’s most recent national conference , held in Adelaide in July, delegates approved language, saying: “Labor will seek, in the short term, to maintain Australia’s government funded humanitarian intake numbers at 20,000 places per year while also continuing to aspire to achieving 27,000 places per year.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Jana Favero, the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre’s deputy chief executive, said lowering the refugee intake would betray people around the world who were relying on Australia. “There are already Australian families desperately waiting to bring loved ones to safety from Iran, Sudan, Gaza and conflicts around the world,” she said. 10:29 One Nation wants to restrict migration. A town in Barnaby Joyce’s electorate welcomes it – video “What makes this even more disturbing is the politics behind it. The government appears increasingly willing to let One Nation dictate the terms of the migration debate, even when that means abandoning commitments made by its own party just weeks ago.” Paul Power, of the Refugee Council of Australia, said the proposed cut went against pledges made by the government at home and abroad. “When the Albanese government increased the refugee and humanitarian program to 20,000 places in 2023, there was no hint that this was a short-term increase. “Until now, Australia has been the only OECD country with a significant refugee resettlement program not to cut places in the past two years. Such a cut would make little difference to Australia’s net overseas migration but be devastating for people seeking a path to safety.” The Greens’ immigration spokesperson David Shoebridge said punishing vulnerable people was a backward step for the country. “The difference between One Nation and Labor is that, when One Nation attacks refugees, they don’t then pat themselves on the back for how much they support multiculturalism,” he said. Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty Images View image in fullscreen McKee closed the Washington bridge in December 2023, which carried about 100,000 vehicles a day, after inspectors found serious structural issues. Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty Images Rhode Island Rhode Island’s Democratic governor loses primary amid anger over bridge Helena Foulkes beats incumbent Dan McKee after criticizing handling of Providence’s Washington bridge, now expected to be completed in 2028 Lauren Gambino Wed 9 Sep 2026 22.05 EDT First published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 20.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Rhode Island’s Dan McKee became the first sitting governor to lose a primary in nearly a decade, bested not by a more progressive challenger or a more youthful upset but by frustration over a bridge. McKee lost his Democratic primary to Helena Foulkes, a former longtime executive with Rhode Island-based retail pharmacy CVS, the Associated Press said on Wednesday. “Tonight, we may have won the Democratic primary for governor, but let me be clear about what happens next: you will have a governor for everyone,” Foulkes said during her victory speech in the state’s capital, Providence. “Because there is so much work that needs to be done, and we need to do this together.” It is rare for a sitting governor to lose a primary election. It hasn’t happened in Rhode Island since 1994. In his concession speech, also in Providence, McKee promised to work with Foulkes to ensure she is elected in November. “This is something that I think is difficult to deal with,” McKee said, “but we just got to hold our heads high.” Several Democratic incumbents have been toppled this cycle, in a wave of anti-establishment anger that has elevated young and progressive insurgents. But this contest was different. On the campaign trail, Foulkes criticized McKee’s handling of repair work on Providence’s Washington bridge, a major east-west traffic artery that carries roughly 100,000 vehicles per day. She accused him of bungling those repairs, which have dragged on longer than originally planned. McKee closed the bridge in December 2023, after inspectors uncovered serious structural problems. By March 2024, officials had concluded that repairing the structure was not feasible and that it would have to be rebuilt. State officials initially estimated that the bridge would be reopened to traffic this year, but the project’s completion date has since been delayed to November 2028 . The primary contest was something of a rematch from four years ago, when Foulkes, who is the niece of former Democratic Senator Chris Dodd of Connecticut, came in a close second behind McKee in a five-way contest. McKee went on to easily win the general election in 2022, after having assumed the role from then-governor Gina Raimondo, who stepped down to become Joe Biden’s US commerce secretary in 2021. Election prognosticators rate the seat as strongly Democratic, and therefore the winner of Wednesday’s primary is seen as having a major advantage in the November general election. Mckee’s defeat was not the only electoral upset on Wednesday. In Providence, David Morales, a 27-year-old Democratic socialist defeated mayor Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary, ending the incumbent’s bid for a second term. Morales’s campaign was backed by progressive stalwarts, including senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and several labor unions. https://www.dw.com/en/un-sounds-the-alar.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ohsa The Israeli military demolished homes in Hebron after a deadly attack there killed two Israeli soldiers [FILE: October 23, 2026] Image: Ammar Awad/REUTERS Advertisement The Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron was met with sharp criticism from the head of the UN as well as the UN's human rights commissioner in comments made on Monday. The criticism comes after an Israeli military operation was launched in the occupied West Bank in response to a shootout on Friday that left two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen dead. Three more Israeli soldiers were also injured. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the military to demolish buildings in the West Bank city of Hebron and to close off the West Bank. It came just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday. What did the UN say about Israeli operation in the West Bank? The United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that "settlements are expanding, evictions are unrelenting with Palestinians driven from their lands," in a post on X. "We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment, with the spectre of ethnic cleaning looming ever larger," he wrote. The UN Human Rights High Commissioner Volker Türk also issued a statement condemning Israeli actions, saying the "aggressive operation" has resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely." "Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing," he said. Israeli army demolishes Palestinian buildings in Hebron To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video A UN report, also released on Monday, that accuses Israel of committing war crimes in the West Bank , was rejected by the Israeli Foreign Ministry as "propaganda." The ministry said that the findings were "not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens." What is the Israeli operation in the West Bank? Israeli troops entered the Deir Baha neighborhood, where the assailants lived, and ordered residents to pack up and leave. The Hebron municipality said that more than 3,000 people, including 200 babies, were ordered to leave. The Israeli military said at the weekend that its troops were carrying out precise, targeted and thorough searches to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure and locate weapons, alongside questioning suspects" in Hebron. The military said the operation was expected to continue "for several days" and would focus on Deir Baha. The largescale response to the firefight in the West Bank comes in the run-up to elections in Israel on Tuesday that could bring an end to Netanyahu's premiership. Netanyahu has frequently painted himself as the only person who can keep Israel safe but his opponents have accused him of lacking a plan.
